items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Earl Hines was a part of that also. Those bands were all coming out of one another...

ctx.x: Earl Hines was a part of that also. Those bands were all coming out of one another, and a lot of the music that was played in each band was coming from the band before. Then they would build a repertoire from there. But they were all – Dizzy and them had a lot of experience playing in all these bands. So that’s what made it possible for them to go into this new kind of music that took technical genius to play.

You talked about touring, some of the bands that you’ve played with, and a sense of the emerging new music. But it was also a time in which you could, as you cited with dances – you’d hear the swing. You’d hear the more advanced modern music. And if there’s a Louis Jordan there, you’re hearing something else. You’re hearing jump swing or some other variation, some other genre. Then you do things later in your career, like with Buddy Johnson, with Lloyd Price, even Motown, because as time goes on, the separations…
